A_target.statement:
Let $R$ be a [[Definition:Ring with Unity|ring with unity]].
An $R$-[[Definition:Module|module]] $Q$ is [[Definition:Injective Module|injective]] {{iff}} for every [[Definition:Submodule|submodule]] $A \subseteq B$ and [[Definition:Module Homomorphism|homomorphism]] $f: A \to Q$, there exists $g: B \to Q$ with $g \restriction_A = f$.

B_source.statement: An $R$-[[Definition:Module|module]] $P$ is [[Definition:Projective Module|projective]] {{iff}} for every [[Definition:Surjection|surjection]] $\pi: B \to C$ and homomorphism $f: P \to C$, there exists $g: P \to B$ with $\pi \circ g = f$.

substitutions.lifting a map out of the module: extending a map into the module

object_map.reformulation: Reverse the arrows of the defining lifting diagram, turning surjections into injections and lifting into extension.

validity_conditions: The two definitions differ exactly by reversing every arrow in the defining diagram, which is what duality means in an abelian category.
Dualizing definitions is automatic, but dualizing theorems is not: each dual statement needs its own proof, since a category and its opposite need not both be module categories.
The asymmetry shows in the examples: free modules are always projective, whereas the injective analogue requires divisibility rather than freeness.
proof_plan: Write projectivity as a lifting diagram: $f: P \to C$ lifts along the surjection $\pi: B \to C$.

Reverse every arrow.
The surjection $\pi: B \to C$ becomes an injection $\iota: A \to B$.
The reversed diagram reads: every $f: A \to Q$ extends along $\iota$ to $g: B \to Q$ with $g \circ \iota = f$.

This is [[Definition:Injective Module|injectivity]].
Theorems proved purely diagrammatically dualize, such as [[Definition:Exact Functor|exactness]] of $\map {\operatorname {Hom} } {-, Q}$.
Those using [[Definition:Free Module|free modules]], such as "every module is a quotient of a projective", need a separate argument, such as [[Baer's Criterion]].
{{qed}}
